item.title: Weekend nor’easter likely to bring damaging winds, coastal flooding
item.description:
Weekend nor’easter likely to bring damaging winds, coastal flooding
September 25, 2026

Forecasters at NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS) are monitoring a powerful nor’easter bringing damaging wind gusts and dangerous coastal flooding to the Northeast this weekend. The New York City metro area and New Jersey may be especially impacted by this storm.

A rapidly deepening storm along the East Coast will likely produce very gusty winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding along the I-95 corridor from the Mid-Atlantic through New England on Saturday and Sunday.

The strongest wind gusts and widespread coastal flooding are most likely near the waterfront and shorelines of New Jersey, New York City and Long Island. The worst flooding is expected with the daytime high tide cycles Saturday and Sunday. Flooding will also extend inland from the waterfront along tidal rivers and bays. 

Prepare now

For the most recent forecast information, go to weather.gov and input in your Zip Code or City, State to access hazardous weather alerts, as well as the latest forecast from the local National Weather Service office in your area. 

Visit NOAA’s Weather Prediction Center for the latest key messages on this nor’easter and its impacts. 

Make sure you have food, water, medications and other basic necessities for yourself, your family and your pets to sufficiently ride out the storm and its aftermath. 

Stay informed on social

Join NOAA’s NWS on social media to stay up to date on the latest weather developments:

  • Find @NWS on X , on Bluesky at nws.noaa.gov, on Facebook and on Instagram.
  • Find and follow your local NOAA National Weather Service forecast office on social media.

item.title: NOAA’s flood mapping tool now covers nearly 100% of U.S.
item.description:
NOAA’s flood mapping tool now covers nearly 100% of U.S.
Experimental Flood Inundation Mapping provides valuable guidance for decision-makers and public
September 24, 2026

NOAA’s National Weather Service announced today that Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM), a revolutionary tool for predicting river flooding, is now available on an experimental basis to nearly 100% of the U.S. population. This is a massive expansion from FIM’s prior coverage of 60% of the country. 

FIM produces estimates of land area covered in water based on model forecast river flows and current conditions that predict where flooding impacts may occur in the following days. It’s a tool for forecasters, emergency managers and the public that alerts users to the latest river and stream flooding conditions. 

“Inundation maps are a critical tool for assessing the impacts of flooding,” said NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs, Ph.D. “NOAA prioritized expanding FIM to ensure that nearly every American can access detailed information beyond the expected river crest height. These maps further support NOAA's mission to protect lives, safeguard property, and strengthen our national economy.”

FIM puts river and stream flooding on the map at a neighborhood scale. It depicts flooding potential along 3.3 million river miles throughout the continental U.S., U.S. territories and Hawaii. For the most recent expansion, FIM’s new coverage areas include: the southeastern U.S. coast and Florida; Great Lakes region; New England; the Rocky Mountains; the Dakotas; and western Nebraska.

Making a difference from day one

FIM has already helped the NWS understand, assess and communicate maximum river flood potential to emergency management personnel, medical care facilities, and other critical decision makers. Success stories from local NWS offices include: 

  • NWS’s office in Nashville, TN used FIM to provide a Senior Assisted Living facility in Macon County information to safely evacuate residents in the spring of 2025, hours before floodwaters reached their doors.
  • In April 2025, NWS office in Little Rock, Arkansas shared FIM with the city of Hardy, who went door to door to evacuate residents. The city reported a nearly 100% success rate in evacuations, saving lives. 
  • As storms rapidly developed in central Texas over the weekend of July 4-7, 2025, the NWS office in Austin/San Antonio distributed FIM to Emergency Management in Georgetown, TX, allowing them to close roads and evacuate residents.
  • In January 2025, the NWS local office in Shreveport, LA noted a large river rise imminent at the Glover River in Oklahoma. FIM allowed local emergency personnel to evacuate residents before the river rose.
  • The Muskegon River in Michigan experienced major to record flooding in April 2026. The NWS office in Grand Rapids used FIM as a critical awareness tool in areas with little additional guidance.  


"FIM has been a game changer when briefing emergency managers, first responders, and communities facing flood risk," said National Weather Service Director Ken Graham. “It helps focus their response on the extent of flooding by using a strong and precise visualization tool.” 

About NOAA’s Flood Inundation Mapping 

FIM services first launched in 2023 covering 10% of the U.S. population and reached 60% in 2025. This latest expansion covering nearly 100% of U.S. residents does not yet cover northern and western portions of Alaska, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa. Expanded FIM maps are publicly available on the National Water Prediction Service website, in several GIS applications available in multiple file types. 

Four versions of FIM are available in near-real time for the Lower 48 states and parts of south-central Alaska:

  • National Water Model hourly analysis of current conditions
  • National Water Model five-day inundation forecast
  • NWS River Forecast Center (RFC) five-day inundation forecast
  • Static “categorical” FIM (CatFIM) for select NWS River Forecast Points

FIM services for Hawaii, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands include:

  • National Water Model hourly analysis of current conditions
  • National Water Model 48-hour inundation forecast
  • Static “categorical” FIM (CatFIM) for select points at gauged locations

NOAA’s Office of Water Prediction (OWP) is a division of the National Weather Service. In partnership with NWS national, regional and local offices, the OWP coordinates, integrates and supports consistent water prediction activities from global to local levels.

item.title: The Great Miami Hurricane of 1926: 100 Years of Hurricane Forecasting and Research
item.description:
The Great Miami Hurricane of 1926: 100 Years of Hurricane Forecasting and Research
September 21, 2026
Predicting extreme weather events and warning the public was much more difficult before we had satellites, aircraft reconnaissance, computer models, radio, television, and the internet. In this talk, we will discuss the Great Miami Hurricane of 1926 and its effects, our understanding of weather and the state of forecasting at the time, what we learned from this event, and how we have advanced in the following 100 years.

This presentation is part of the NOAA Heritage Week 2026 Speaker Series.

item.title: NOAA announces 2026 federal recreational red snapper season, exempted fishing permits in South Atlantic
item.description:
NOAA announces 2026 federal recreational red snapper season, exempted fishing permits in South Atlantic
September 22, 2026

NOAA Fisheries announced today the 2026 federal recreational red snapper fishing season in the South Atlantic and the issuance of three exempted fishing permits (EFPs) to Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina. 

The federal recreational red snapper season will open for three days this year from October 9 through October 11 —one day longer than last year’s two-day recreational season. 

In addition, NOAA Fisheries has issued EFPs to Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina authorizing extended recreational red snapper fishing seasons for eligible participants from October 9 through October 22. After a comprehensive view of the October season and additional information, NOAA Fisheries and the states will jointly determine whether a second season may take place in December 2026. NOAA’s EFPs allow states to pilot test new data collection and management strategies for the recreational harvest of red snapper in state and federal waters in 2026. 

“NOAA is dedicated to working with our state partners, fishermen, and fishery managers to advance sustainable fisheries and strengthen the science that supports them,” said Neil Jacobs, Ph.D, NOAA administrator. “These efforts enable us to test new, innovative approaches and improve recreational data collection to support the long-term sustainability of South Atlantic red snapper.” 

“Recreational fishermen and the states play an indispensable role in helping us better understand and manage the South Atlantic red snapper fishery,” said Eugenio Piñeiro Soler, assistant administrator for NOAA Fisheries. "These pilot projects provide a great opportunity to strengthen our data and inform future management approaches.” 

NOAA Fisheries is working closely with the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council offsite link and states to rebuild the red snapper stock and investigate ways to reduce recreational discards. The goal is to work collaboratively with the states to improve the collection of recreational fishing data; expand insights into effort, catch, and discards; and to evaluate the potential benefits of state-specific management strategies while maintaining catches and discards within sustainable levels and informing long-term, state-led management. 

Find out more from NOAA Fisheries regarding each state’s EFP.

item.title: NOAA selects Tomorrow.io to help advance U.S. weather forecasting
item.description:
NOAA selects Tomorrow.io to help advance U.S. weather forecasting
September 17, 2026

NOAA has selected Tomorrow.io to provide contracting support for the Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC), the backbone of NOAA’s operational weather forecast modeling suite. This contract advances NOAA’s historic effort to accelerate the development of NOAA’s next-generation Earth modeling system, the Unified Forecast System (UFS), through open science.

“With EPIC, we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to cement U.S. leadership in weather prediction by leveraging the full power of the public, private, and academic sectors,” said NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs, Ph.D. “We will accelerate the transition of scientific research into operations through a unified approach to model development in a cloud-based environment, which will advance our mission of protecting life and property.”

Established in 2019, the EPIC program provides community modeling infrastructure and engagement opportunities to foster collaboration with the larger weather research enterprise – including academia, public agencies, and private industry. The program aims to more efficiently transition research innovations into operational forecast models used by NOAA’s National Weather Service. 

While the EPIC program is in charge of tasks related to management and planning, scientific innovation, and other relevant projects, this contracting partner is responsible for software infrastructure and engineering, as well as user support services. The company will share responsibility for engaging the UFS community and collaborating on high-performance computing initiatives. 

The goal of the UFS is to modernize and streamline NOAA’s operational modeling suite while accelerating the transition of scientific research into operations through a unified, community-driven Earth modeling system. By providing a single, flexible framework that integrates various components — such as the atmosphere, ocean and land — the UFS replaces numerous standalone operational models to better predict weather and climate across all timescales.

“This partnership with Tomorrow.io is another key step in EPIC’s goal of advancing the UFS toward a fully coupled Earth System Model,” said Ken Graham, director, NOAA’s National Weather Service. “This is a major component of the Weather Service’s transformation effort, which will help ensure America is ready, responsive, and resilient to extreme weather and water events.”

With this new contract, Tomorrow.io will provide critical modeling infrastructure and community engagement support as NOAA integrates the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), the computational heart of NOAA’s next-generation weather modeling system, into the UFS. Once incorporated with the UFS, MPAS will serve as the main engine for predicting atmospheric movements—everything from local thunderstorms and tornadoes to tropical hurricanes, jet streams, and major global weather patterns. 

“We are proud to lead the team supporting EPIC and NOAA, the trusted global authority in weather science, in strengthening the nation’s forecasting models and infrastructure,” said Thomas Cavett, vice president, U.S. Federal Business, for Tomorrow.io offsite link. “Our expertise in AI modeling and satellite observations reflects our commitment to NOAA’s mission of protecting lives and property. We look forward to helping realize NOAA’s vision and supporting continued progress in forecasting and early warning for partner nations around the world.”

More about EPIC

EPIC is a national priority supported by the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act offsite link of 2017, which calls for NOAA to prioritize improving weather data, modeling, computing, forecasting, and warnings for the protection of life and property and to enhance the national economy. Congress authorized EPIC and further called for NOAA to accelerate community-developed scientific and technological advances to its operational numerical weather prediction in the National Integrated Drought Information System Reauthorization Act offsite link of 2018 (Public Law 115-423).
